background.definition: Von Willebrand Diease (VWD) is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand Factor (VWF).

list.listitem: Varies from 0.6% to 1.3% of the general population, or an estimated 3 million persons in the United States.
VWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder.
A typical generalist physician will see at least one case every few years.
Mutations in the von Willebrand Factor (VWF) gene result in deficiency or dysfunction of VWF.
However, there are mutations in other genes that results in low VWF levels, thus genetic testing is not generally recommended except perhaps for type 2 variants and type 3 VWD.
Von Willebrand Factor is important for the primary hemostatic response to vascular injury (platelet adhesion and aggregation).
Deficiency or dysfunction of VWF thus results in mucutaneous type bleeding.
Severe deficiency of VWF (Type 3 VWD) results in spontaneous mucocutaneous, soft tissue and joint bleeding.

Suspect VWD in persons with more than 5 nosebleeds per year, when bleeding from simple cut lasts more than 10 minutes, if family members have bleeding problem, heavy bleeding with dental and other surgery, or heavy menstrual bleeding. C
A detailed hemostatic history is the best tool for deciding which patients need laboratory testing for VWD (see ). C
Initial diagnostic tests include von Willebrand factor antigen (VWF:Ag), VWF activity (ristocetin cofactor; VWF:RCo) and factor VIII activity (FVIII:C). C

Differential.Differential_Features: X-linked recessive inheritance, whereas VWD Type 2 N is autosomal

list.listitem: See for classification of VWD.

Suspect VWD in persons with more than 5 nosebleeds per year, when bleeding from simple cut lasts more than 10 minutes, if family members have bleeding problem, heavy bleeding with dental and other surgery, or heavy menstrual bleeding.

The bleeding pattern in VWD is typically mucocutaneous: frequent and prolonged epistaxis (38%-62%), prolonged or recurrent bleeding from trivial wounds (36%), menorrhagia in women (47%-60%), blood in stools or urine (14%), frequent and large spontaneous bruises or bruises occuring after minimal trauma (50%), and gingival bleeding (30%). Hemarthrosis in VWD is relatively uncommon (6%-8%) except in patients with severe Type 3 VWD (35%-45%).
Bleeding in association with surgery may include bleeding after wisdom tooth removal, after child birth in women, or after tonsillectomy or other minor or major surgery.

A detailed personal and family hemostatic history is the best initial diagnostic tool for detection of bleeding disorders (see for suggested questions). Identify spontaneity, severity, sites and duration of bleeding, ease with which bleeding can be stopped. Also inquire about presence or absence of family history of bleeding disorders. Women with menorrhagia should have VWD excluded.
Physical examination: look for presence of ecchymoses and hematomas.
The presence of abnormal bleeding or hemostasis in the history and physical examination should prompt laboratory testing including PT, PTT and platelet count.

Initial tests for diagnosis of VWD include von Willebrand factor antigen (VWF:Ag), von Willbrand factor activity also called ristocetin cofactor activity (VWF:RCo), factor VIII activity (FVIII:C) and ABO blood typing.

If the initial testing raises the possibility of VWD, then additional testing to classify the type of VWD should be performed. VWF multimer analysis is used to determine the distribution of VWF multimer.
The low dose ristocetin induced platelet aggregation aids in diagnosis of Type 2B VWD.
The VWF:Factor VIII binding assay distinguishes mild congenital hemophilia A from VWD Type 2 N (Normandy).
Bleeding time is not available in many institutions and is of limited value. A prolonged bleeding time is only 42% sensitive for detection of VWD.
The platelet function analyzer (PFA-100) has varying sensitivity for VWD, only 61% in one good quality study.

Data from a cohort of patients with VWF levels between 0.31 and 0.60 IU/ml was used to develop a simple risk score for the likelihood of bleeding requiring treatment (post-surgical, post-partum, and traumatic or spontaneous bleeding): 1 point for age <18 years at diagnosis, 2 points for abnormal bleeding score at diagnosis, and 2 points if referred for personal bleeding diathesis. Those with 0 or 1 points had a 6.3% bleeding rate, those with 2 points a 13% rate, and those with 3 to 5 points a 23% rate.
Evaluate bleeding symptoms by history and examination, and take a family history of bleeding disorders.

If there is concern for presence of bleeding disorder (presence of spontaneous bleeding or bleeding after minimal trauma or minor or major surigical procedures) see for evaluation of patients with suspected VWD.
Type 1 VWD: DDAVP (desmopressin) trial and if responsive, use for minor bleeding and procedures. B
Types 2 and 3 VWD: purfied plasma derived concentrate. B
Ensure that patients wear medical identifiers and carry their treatment guidelines. C

Type 1 VWD: Perform a DDAVP (desmopressin) trial in patients with VWF:RCo greater than 10%. The purpose is to determine response to DDAVP; if responsive, it can be utilized for minor bleeding, minor procedures, and management of menorrhagia in lieu of plasma derived VWF concentrates. Note that frequent (e.g. daily) administration of DDAVP can result in hyponatremia, hypotention, seizures. For such situations, plasma derived VWF concentrates should be used (e.g. for major sugery). A DDAVP trial is not generally indicated for patients with Type 3 VWD and Type 2 variants, but may be considered in Type 2 patients with VWF:RCo greater than 10%.

The dose of DDAVP is 0.3 mcg/kg IV. It can be given as intranasal desmopressin acetate (Stimate). For persons less than 50 kg the dose is one puff (150 mcg), while for persons greater than 50 kg it is two puffs (150 mcg each, one in each nostril). Caution: do not use the DDAVP formulation tyically used for bed wetting (0.1 mg/mL).
Currently, DDAVP is contraindicated in Type 2B VWD, given the worsening of the thrombocytopenia that can occur.

Antifibrinolytic agents (epsilon amino caproic acid) are typically used in conjuction with DDAVP (for patients who are responsive) for minor surgical procedures e.g. dental extractions, colon polypectomy.
For patients with Type 2 and 3 VWD, plasma derived, purified VWF concentrates are used for prophylaxis and management of bleeding.

Consider prophylactic infusions (e.g. once or twice weekly) of VWF concentrate for patients with Type 3 VWD who experience frequent spontanous bleeding. In general, daily administration of VWF concentrates in other subtypes of VWDare not indicated.
Short term infusions are needed in the perioperative setting.
Topical thrombin is used as an adjunct for management of dental procedures.
Once the diagnosis of VWD is established, all patients should wear medical identification identifying their bleeding disorder and should receive hepatitis A and B immunization series.
A patient with bleeding symptoms may be referred to a comprehensive hemohilia center for a cost-effective diagnostic workup.

At diagnosis, the patient should be referred to a comprehensive hemophilia center for development of a personalized treatment plan. This plan should be shared with the primary care physician, the patient and local emergency rooms.
Majority of bleeding episodes can be managed as an outpatient; however, hospitalization for major bleeding, trauma and surgery should be considered.

Close monitoring of VWF levels are important for cost effective utilization of VWF concentrates. Thus, surgery in such patients should be performed in hospitals with access to expertise in management of bleeding disorders and relatively rapid turnaround times of VWF assays.
During hospitalization for management of bleeding or surgery, VWF assays should be used for close monitoring of VWF concentrates.
Majority of patients with Type 1 and 2 variants of VWD have mild bleeding symptoms and do not experience major spontaneous hemorrhages. B
Type 3 VWD patients experience frequent spontaneous bleeds. B

With annual follow up in conjunction with a comprehensive hemophilia center, patients have good long term outcomes, as documented in patients with hemophilia, from the standpoint of decreased hospitalizations from bleeding complications. B
Between 2% and 30% of patients have arthropathy as a result of VWD.
In patients with atrial fibrillation, increased circulating levels of van Willebrand factor are associated with an increased risk for death or major adverse cardiovascular events.
VWF levels increase with age, but the protein remains dysfunctional.
Thus, DDAVP or VWF concentrates may be requred for management of hemorrhage and surgery even though VWF levels may be normal.

Because VWF levels rise with gestational age especially in the second and third trimester, diagnostic testing should be performed prior to pregnancy or if performed during pregnancy, should be repeated 6 to 8 weeks post partum. Antenatal management: DDAVP or VWF factor concentrates for VWD patients who are bleeding. Management of labor and delivery: VWF levels of at least 50% or more should be achieved and maintained for at least 5 days postpartum. Regional anaesthesia is safe at these levels. Postpartum management: delayed postpartum bleeding is common and VWF levels should be monitored and maintained at 50% or higher levels for at least 5 days postpartum. However, in deliveries complicated by hemorrhage VWF levels should be maintained at 50% or higher for a longer period of time.
Children with Type 3 VWD who require frequent infusions of VWF concentrates typically require placement of a central venous cather (e.g. Port-a-cath) for ease of factor infusions.

feature.caption: Suggested Initial Questions to Identify Patients with a Bleeding Disorder.
feature.feature_body: Do you have a blood relative who has a bleeding disorder, such as von Willebrand disease or hemophilia? Have you ever had prolonged bleeding from trivial wounds, lasting more than 15 minutes or recurring spontaneously during the 7 days after the wound? Have you ever had heavy, prolonged, or recurrent bleeding after surgical procedures, such as tonsillectomy? Have you ever had bruising, with minimal or no apparent trauma, especially if you could feel a lump under the bruise? Have you ever had a spontaneous nosebleed that required more than 10 minutes to stop or needed medical attention? Have you ever had heavy, prolonged, or recurrent bleeding after dental extractions that required medical attention? Have you ever had blood in your stool, unexplained by a specific anatomic lesion (such as an ulcer in the stomach, or a polyp in the colon), that required medical attention? Have you ever had anemia requiring treatment or received blood transfusion? For women: have you ever had heavy menses, characterized by the presence of clots greater than an inch in diameter and/or changing a pad or tampon more than hourly, or resulting in anemia or low iron level? From Nichols WL, Hultin MB, James AH, et al. von Willebrand disease (VWD): evidence-based diagnosis and management guidelines, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) Expert Panel report (USA).
